1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4 Bc5 5..strategy: Castles first and offers the pawn on d4 for a lead in development, planning to play c3 later, when ...Bb4+ no longer wins a tempo. The positions that follow are sharp, with both kings exposed.

Attacks f7 a second time while Black cannot yet castle. But a developed knight moves again with the queen still at home, so the line is thought premature, and Black defends with the g8-knight, after which White must work to keep the initiative.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4 Bc5 5..name: Scotch Game: Scotch Gambit, Sarratt Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4 Bc5 5..background: Long considered inferior, perhaps because of the well-known game Meek-Morphy, Mobile 1855, it has since appeared in grandmaster play.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4 Bc5 5..strategy: The standard defence: the knight develops, though from the rim, and guards f7, so the double attack is met without a king move. Black is ready to give material back at the right moment and keeps a solid position.
Opts for solidity: the pawn supports the bishop on c5 and shuts out the e5 thrust that 5...Nf6 would allow, and it frees the c8-bishop. Black keeps the extra pawn for now and goes for a sound set-up.
Develops with a hit on e4, but it allows White to push e5 with tempo. The resulting open game is double-edged and considered good for White, so the natural move is not the safest here.
